question:
An international insurance company has clients all across the globe. The company has financial files that are stored in an Amazon S3 bucket which is behind CloudFront. At present, their clients can access their data by directly using an S3 URL or using their CloudFront distribution. The company wants to deliver their content to a specific client in California and they need to make sure that only that client can access the data.

Which of the following options is a valid solution that meets the above requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Use CloudFront Signed Cookies to ensure that only their client can access the files. Enable HTTPS in your CloudFront distribution.
Use CloudFront signed URLs to ensure that only their client can access the files. Enable field-level encryption in your CloudFront distribution.

Create a new S3 bucket in US West (N. California) region and upload the files. Use S3 pre-signed URLs to ensure that only their client can access the files. Remove permission to use Amazon S3 URLs to read the files for anyone else.

Create a new S3 bucket in US West (N. California) region and upload the files. Set up an origin access control (OAC) and give it permission to read the files in the bucket. Enable HTTPS in your CloudFront distribution.

Use CloudFront signed URLs to ensure that only their client can access the files. Create an origin access control (OAC) and give it permission to read the files in the bucket. Remove permission to use Amazon S3 URLs to read the files for anyone else.

explanation.text:
Options <<3>> and <<5>> are the intended mechanisms for limited-time private content delivery: an authorized backend issues an S3 presigned URL or a CloudFront signed URL for a permitted object. Keep the origin private and scope permissions, expiry, and any KMS access correctly. Both URLs are bearer credentials: anyone who obtains a still-valid URL can ordinarily use it. They do not cryptographically bind access to the originally named client, and they do not prevent saving or redistributing already downloaded content. When non-transferable user authorization is required, add a request-time authenticated application layer. The answer assumes controlled URL distribution rather than a guarantee against recipient sharing.

question:
A company recently switched to using Amazon CloudFront for its content delivery network. The development team already made the preparations necessary to optimize the application performance for global users. The company’s content management system (CMS) serves both dynamic and static content. The dynamic content is served from a fleet of Amazon EC2 instances behind an application load balancer (ALB) while the static assets are served from an Amazon S3 bucket. The ALB is configured as the default origin of the CloudFront distribution. An Origin Access Control (OAC) was created and applied to the S3 bucket policy to allow access only from the CloudFront distribution. Upon testing the CMS webpage, the static assets return an error 404 message.

Which of the following solutions must be implemented to solve this error? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Edit the CloudFront distribution and create another origin for serving the static assets.
Update the application load balancer listener and create a new path-based rule for the static assets so that it will forward requests to the Amazon S3 bucket.

Replace the CloudFront distribution with AWS Global Accelerator. Configure the AWS Global Accelerator with multiple endpoint groups that target endpoints on all AWS Regions. Use the accelerator’s static IP address to create a record in Amazon Route 53 for the apex domain.
Update the CloudFront distribution and create a new behavior that will forward to the origin of the static assets based on path pattern.
Update the application load balancer listener to check for HEADER condition if the request is from CloudFront and forward it to the Amazon S3 bucket.

explanation.text:
Amazon CloudFront is a web service that speeds up the distribution of your static and dynamic web content, such as .html, .css, .js, and image files, to your users. CloudFront delivers your content through a worldwide network of data centers called edge locations. When a user requests content that you’re serving with CloudFront, the request is routed to the edge location that provides the lowest latency (time delay) so that content is delivered with the best possible performance.

You create a CloudFront distribution to tell CloudFront where you want the content to be delivered from and the details about how to track and manage content delivery. Then CloudFront uses computers—edge servers—that are close to your viewers to deliver that content quickly when someone wants to see it or use it.

In general, if you’re using an Amazon S3 bucket as the origin for a CloudFront distribution, you can either allow everyone to have access to the files there or you can restrict access. To restrict access to content that you serve from Amazon S3 buckets, follow these steps:

1. Create a special CloudFront user called an origin access control (OAC) and associate it with your distribution.
2. Configure your S3 bucket permissions so that CloudFront can use the OAC to access the files in your bucket and serve them to your users. Make sure that users can’t use a direct URL to the S3 bucket to access a file there.

After you take these steps, users can only access your files through CloudFront, not directly from the S3 bucket.

You can configure a single CloudFront web distribution to serve different types of requests from multiple origins. For example, if you are building a website that serves static content from an Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket and dynamic content from a load balancer, you can serve both types of content from a CloudFront web distribution.

Follow these steps to configure a CloudFront web distribution to serve static content from an S3 bucket and dynamic content from a load balancer:

1. Open your web distribution from the CloudFront console.
2. Choose the Origins tab.
3. Create one origin for your S3 bucket and another origin for your load balancer.
 Note: If you’re using a custom origin server or an S3 website endpoint, you must enter the origin’s domain name into the Origin Domain Name field.
4. From your distribution, choose the Behaviors tab.
5. Create a behavior that specifies a path pattern to route all static content requests to the S3 bucket. For example, you can set the “images/*.jpg” path pattern to route all requests for “.jpg” files in the images directory to the S3 bucket.
6. Edit the Default (*) path pattern behavior and set its Origin as your load balancer.

Therefore, the correct answers are:

– Edit the CloudFront distribution and create another origin for serving the static assets.

– Update the CloudFront distribution and create a new behavior that will forward to the origin of the static assets based on path pattern.

The option that says: Update the application load balancer listener and create a new path-based rule for the static assets so that it will forward requests to the Amazon S3 bucket is incorrect. The OAC is used to allow only CloudFront to access the static assets on the S3 bucket. Using the load balancer to forward the requests will result in the access denied error.

The option that says: Replace the CloudFront distribution with AWS Global Accelerator. Configure the AWS Global Accelerator with multiple endpoint groups that target endpoints on all AWS Regions. Use the accelerator’s static IP address to create a record in Amazon Route 53 for the apex domain is incorrect. AWS Global Accelerator is a network layer service that improves the availability and performance of your applications used by a wide global audience. This service is not a substitute for a CDN service like Amazon CloudFront.

The option that says: Update the application load balancer listener to check for HEADER condition if the request is from CloudFront and forward it to the Amazon S3 bucket is incorrect. Although an ALB can inspect the HTTP Header requests, using the load balancer to forward the requests will result in the access denied error because of the OAC on the S3 bucket policy.

question:
A company is migrating an interactive car registration web system hosted on its on-premises network to AWS Cloud. The current architecture of the system consists of a single NGINX web server and a MySQL database running on a Fedora server, which both reside in its on-premises data center. For the new cloud architecture, a load balancer must be used to evenly distribute the incoming traffic to the application servers. Amazon Route 53 must be used for both domain registration and domain management.

In this scenario, what would be the most efficient way to transfer the web application to AWS?

options.text:
1. Use the AWS Transform MGN to create an EC2 AMI of the NGINX web server.
 2. Configure auto-scaling to launch in two Availability Zones.
 3. Launch a multi-AZ MySQL Amazon RDS instance in one availability zone only.
 4. Import the data into Amazon RDS from the latest MySQL backup.
 5. Create an ELB to front your web servers
 6. Use Route 53 and create an A record pointing to the elastic load balancer.

1. Launch two NGINX EC2 instances in two Availability Zones.
 2. Copy the web files from the on-premises web server to each Amazon EC2 web server, using Amazon S3 as the repository.
 3. Migrate the database using the AWS Database Migration Service.
 4. Create an ELB to front your web servers.
 5. Use Route 53 and create an alias A record pointing to the ELB.

1. Use AWS Transform to automatically migrate the existing NGINX web server from the on-premises Fedora server to AWS.
 2. Configure Auto Scaling to launch two web servers in two Availability Zones.
 3. Launch a Multi-AZ MySQL Amazon Relational Database Service (RDS) instance in one Availability Zone only.
 4. Import the data into Amazon RDS from the latest MySQL backup.
 5. Use Route 53 to create a private hosted zone and point a non-alias A record to the ELB.

1. Use AWS DataSync to transfer the web files from the on-premises NGINX server to an Amazon S3 bucket.
 2. Run the website directly out of Amazon S3.
 3. Migrate the database using the AWS Database Migration Service and AWS Schema Conversion Tool (AWS SCT).
 4. Use Route 53 and create an alias record pointing to the ELB.

explanation.text:
This is a trick question that contains a lot of information to confuse you, especially if you don’t know the fundamental concepts of AWS. All options seem to be correct except for their last steps in setting up Route 53. The options that have a step to launch a multi-AZ MySQL Amazon RDS instance in one availability zone only are wrong since a Multi-AZ deployment configuration uses multiple Availability Zones.

To route domain traffic to an ELB load balancer, use Amazon Route 53 to create an alias record that points to your load balancer. An alias record is a Route 53 extension to DNS. It’s similar to a CNAME record, but you can create an alias record both for the root domain, such as example.com, and for subdomains, such as www.example.com. (You can create CNAME records only for subdomains). For EC2 instances, always use a Type A Record without an Alias. For ELB, Cloudfront, and S3, always use a Type A Record with an Alias, and finally, for RDS, always use the CNAME Record with no Alias.

AWS Database Migration Service helps you migrate databases to AWS quickly and securely. The source database remains fully operational during the migration, minimizing downtime to applications that rely on the database. The AWS Database Migration Service can migrate your data to and from the most widely used commercial and open-source databases.

Hence, the correct answer is:

1. Launch two NGINX EC2 instances in two Availability Zones.

2. Copy the web files from the on-premises web server to each Amazon EC2 web server, using Amazon S3 as the repository.

3. Migrate the database using the AWS Database Migration Service.

4. Create an ELB to front your web servers.

5. Use Route 53 and create an alias A record pointing to the ELB.

The following sets of options are incorrect because they are just using an A record without an Alias:

1. Use the AWS Transform MGN to create an EC2 AMI of the NGINX web server.

2. Configure auto-scaling to launch in two Availability Zones.

3. Launch a multi-AZ MySQL Amazon RDS instance in one availability zone only.

4. Import the data into Amazon RDS from the latest MySQL backup.

 5. Create an ELB to front your web servers.

6. Use Route 53 and create an A record pointing to the elastic load balancer.

—

1. Use AWS Transform to automatically migrate the existing NGINX web server from the on-premises Fedora server to AWS.

2. Configure Auto Scaling to launch two web servers in two Availability Zones.

3. Launch a Multi-AZ MySQL Amazon Relational Database Service (RDS) instance in one Availability Zone only.

4. Import the data into Amazon RDS from the latest MySQL backup.

5. Use Route 53 to create a private hosted zone and point a non-alias A record to the ELB.

Take note as well that the AWS Transform MGN is primarily used to migrate virtual machines only, which can be from VMware vSphere and Windows Hyper-V to your AWS cloud.

The following option is incorrect because the web system that is being migrated is a non-static (dynamic) website, which cannot be hosted in S3:

1. Use AWS DataSync to transfer the web files from the on-premises NGINX server to an Amazon S3 bucket.

2. Run the website directly out of Amazon S3.

 3. Migrate the database using the AWS Database Migration Service and AWS Schema Conversion Tool (AWS SCT).

4. Use Route 53 and create an alias record pointing to the ELB.

https://aws.amazon.com/cloud-migration/

https://docs.aws.amazon.com/Route53/latest/DeveloperGuide/routing-to-elb-load-balancer.html

question:
A company is running thousands of virtualized Linux and Microsoft Windows servers on its on-premises data center. The virtual servers host a range of Java and PHP applications that use MySQL and Oracle databases. There are also several department services hosted on an external data center. The company uses SAN storage to provide iSCSI disks to its physical servers. The company wants to migrate its data center to the AWS Cloud, but the technical documentation of the systems is incomplete and outdated. The Solutions Architect was tasked to analyze the current environment and estimate the cost of migrating the resources to the cloud.

Which of the following should the Solutions Architect do to effectively plan the cloud migration? (Select THREE.)

options.text: Use the AWS Transform discovery tool to gather information about the running virtual machines and running applications inside the servers.
Use AWS Transform MGN to automate the migration of the on-premises virtual machines to the AWS Cloud.
Use AWS X-Ray to analyze the applications running on the servers and identify possible errors that may be encountered during the migration.
Generate a migration readiness assessment report with the AWS Cloud Adoption Readiness Tool (CART) to highlight gaps in organizational skills and processes.
Use Amazon Inspector to scan and assess the applications deployed on the on-premises virtual machines and save the generated report to an Amazon S3 bucket.
Use AWS Transform migration assessment jobs and workspaces to estimate migration costs, generate right-sizing recommendations, produce reports, and support migration planning.

explanation.text:
The scenario requires tools of services that will help to effectively plan the cloud migration, so the answers should be focused on planning.

AWS Transform is a service designed to accelerate and simplify the transformation of infrastructure, applications, and code through an intelligent AI experience. It offers specialized tools that streamline modernization and migration efforts across various workloads.

With AWS Transform, you can:

– Modernize and migrate IBM z/OS and Fujitsu GS21 to AWS

– Migrate VMware workloads to Amazon EC2

– Modernize .NET applications to Linux-ready cross-platform .NET

– Assess workloads for migration readiness

AWS Transform assists in offloading labor-intensive and complex transformation tasks during the discovery, planning, and execution phases to AI agents with expertise in various languages, frameworks, and infrastructures. This approach allows your teams to focus on innovation while efficiently transforming complex, large-scale projects through a unified web experience.

The AWS Transform discovery tool assists you in automatically discovering the server inventory within your organization in preparation for migration. This tool supports VMware vCenter, Microsoft Hyper-V, and imported servers. To utilize the discovery tool, you need to configure one or more discovery sources, allow the tool to run, and then review the results displayed in the Discovered Inventory pane.

Once you configure a discovery source, the tool will begin collecting information. The time required for the discovery tool to completely analyze your network depends on the size of your environment. For businesses utilizing a directional migration approach, you can leverage the Migration Portfolio Assessment (MPA) files generated by the tool after the server collection is completed.

The AWS Cloud Adoption Readiness Tool (CART) helps organizations of all sizes develop efficient and effective plans for cloud adoption and enterprise cloud migrations. This 16-question online survey and assessment report detail your cloud migration readiness across six perspectives, including business, people, process, platform, operations, and security. Once you complete a CART survey, you can provide your contact details to download a customized cloud migration assessment that charts your readiness and what you can do to improve it. This tool is designed to help organizations assess their progress with cloud adoption and identify gaps in organizational skills and processes.

AWS Transform assessments evaluate the cost, feasibility, and business value of migrating on-premises infrastructure to AWS. These assessments provide automated right-sizing recommendations, multi-scenario comparisons, and interactive refinement through chat.

You can apply migration assessments for several objectives:

– Get cost estimates for Amazon RDS for SQL Server, Amazon EC2, Amazon EBS, Amazon S3, and Amazon FSx

– Receive automated right-sizing recommendations

– Assess business value and sustainability impact

– Compare multiple migration scenarios side by side

– Refine assessments interactively through chat

– Generate executive presentations and detailed reports

Therefore, the correct answers are:

– Use the AWS Transform Discovery Tool to gather information about the running virtual machines and running applications inside the servers.

– Generate a migration readiness assessment report with the AWS Cloud Adoption Readiness Tool (CART) to highlight gaps in organizational skills and processes.

– Use AWS Transform migration assessment jobs and workspaces to estimate migration costs, generate right-sizing recommendations, produce reports, and support migration planning.

The option that says: Use AWS Transform MGN to automate the migration of the on-premises virtual machines to the AWS Cloud is incorrect because MGN is primarily used for the actual migration of your on-premises virtual machines to the AWS Cloud and not for planning. Take note that in the scenario, the Solutions Architect was tasked to analyze the existing on-premises architecture first before doing the actual migration to AWS.

The option that says: Use AWS X-Ray to analyze the applications running on the servers and identify possible errors that may be encountered during the migration is incorrect because AWS X-Ray is typically used to debug production and distributed applications, such as those built using a microservices architecture. This is not helpful for planning the migration.

The option that says: Use Amazon Inspector to scan and assess the applications deployed on the on-premises virtual machines and save the generated report to an Amazon S3 bucket is incorrect because Amazon Inspector is an automated security assessment service that helps improve the security and compliance of applications deployed on AWS. This is not helpful for assessing the applications on the on-premises data center.

question:
A company is migrating a legacy Oracle database from its on-premises data center to AWS. It will be deployed in an existing Amazon EBS backed Amazon EC2 instance with multiple EBS volumes attached. For the migration, a new volume must be created for the Oracle database and then attached to the instance. This will be used by a financial web application and will primarily store historical financial data that are infrequently accessed. The company is also considering using Amazon GuardDuty to monitor its AWS environment for security threats.

Which of the following is the MOST cost-effective and throughput-oriented solution that the Solutions Architect should implement?

options.text: Migrate the database using the AWS Database Migration Service and use a Provisioned IOPS (io1) EBS volume.
Migrate the database using the AWS Database Migration Service and use a Cold HDD (sc1) EBS volume.
Migrate the database using the AWS Transform MGN and use a Throughput Optimized (st1) EBS volume.
Migrate the database using the AWS Transform MGN and use a General Purpose (gp2) EBS Volume.

explanation.text:
Option <<2>> is the intended low-cost choice only for the stated historical, throughput-oriented workload: cold HDD (sc1) is designed for infrequently accessed large sequential I/O, not a general recommendation for Oracle data files. Random IOPS, latency-sensitive queries, or an active transactional workload can make SSD necessary even when access is infrequent. Benchmark the actual query pattern and restore/recovery needs. DMS moves database data into an already configured supported database target; it does not create an Oracle deployment merely by selecting an EBS volume type. EBS snapshots are backups, not directly queryable database storage.

https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ebs/latest/userguide/ebs-volume-types.html

question:
A company plans to migrate its on-premises workload to the AWS cloud. The solutions architect has been tasked to perform a Total Cost of Ownership (TCO) analysis and prepare a cost-optimized migration plan for the systems hosted in your on-premises network to AWS. It is required to collect detail about configuration, usage, and behavioral data from the on-premises servers to help better understand the current workloads before doing the migration.

Which of the following option is the recommended solution that should be implemented to meet the company requirements?

Assume the company is an existing AWS Application Discovery Service customer and remains eligible to use the service.

options.text: Use the AWS SAM service to move your data to AWS which will also help you perform the TCO analysis.
Use the AWS Migration Hub service to collect data from each server in your on-premises data center and perform the TCO analysis.
Use the AWS Application Migration Service (MGN) to migrate VM servers to AWS and collect the data required to complete your TCO analysis.
Use the AWS Application Discovery Service to gather data about your on-premises data center and perform the TCO analysis.

explanation.text:
Option <<4>> applies to an existing AWS Application Discovery Service customer, as explicitly clarified in the stem. Application Discovery Service stopped accepting new customers on October 7, 2025; existing-customer scenarios are not the same as new deployments. For a new assessment, evaluate the current AWS Transform discovery and assessment capabilities or Migration Evaluator rather than assuming ADS can be newly enabled. Discovery collects inventory/utilization/dependency information; a migration replication tool is not automatically a substitute for an assessment/TCO workflow.

question:
A company has a suite of IBM products in its on-premises data centers, such as IBM WebSphere, IBM MQ, and IBM DB2 servers. The solutions architect has been tasked to migrate all of the current systems to the AWS Cloud in the most cost-effective way and improve the availability of the cloud infrastructure.

Which of the following options is the MOST suitable solution that the solutions architect should implement to meet the company’s requirements?

options.text: Use the AWS Application Migration Service to migrate your servers to AWS. Set up Amazon EC2 instances to re-host your IBM WebSphere and IBM DB2 servers separately. Re-host and migrate the IBM MQ service to Amazon SQS Standard Queue.

Use the AWS Database Migration Service (DMS) and the AWS Schema Conversion Tool (SCT) to convert, migrate, and re-architect the IBM Db2 database to Amazon Aurora. Set up an Auto Scaling group of EC2 instances with an ELB in front to migrate and re-host your IBM WebSphere. Migrate and re-platform IBM MQ to Amazon MQ in a phased approach.

Use the AWS Application Migration Service to migrate your servers to AWS. Upload the IBM licenses to AWS License Manager and use the licenses when configuring Amazon EC2 instances to re-host your IBM WebSphere and IBM DB2 servers separately. Re-host and migrate the IBM MQ service to Amazon MQ.

Use the AWS Database Migration Service (DMS) and the AWS Schema Conversion Tool (SCT) to convert, re-architect, and migrate the IBM Db2 database to Amazon Aurora. Set up an Auto Scaling group of EC2 instances with an ELB in front to migrate and re-host your IBM WebSphere. Re-host and migrate the IBM MQ service to Amazon SQS FIFO Queue.

explanation.text:
Option <<2>> is the intended replatforming direction, subject to an explicit compatibility assessment and application changes. Aurora is not a drop-in Db2 engine, and Amazon MQ supports ActiveMQ/RabbitMQ rather than IBM MQ protocol compatibility by assertion. Assess database schema, SQL, procedures, messaging semantics, transactions, and client libraries; use supported schema-conversion and data-migration paths where applicable. A phased migration with change capture and testing can reduce downtime, but does not guarantee it without validating the actual source/target versions and workload. Do not infer that similarly named managed database or messaging services make proprietary middleware automatically portable.

question:
A company is planning to host a two-tier application on AWS. They’ve chosen to use the LAMP (Linux, Apache, MySQL, PHP) stack, wherein a stateful application will run on Amazon EC2 instances, and the database will be managed using Amazon Aurora.

The customer base is expected to grow rapidly, which would likely result in unprecedented traffic spikes. The design must ensure that both the application and the database tiers can scale automatically in response to changes in demand.

Which combination of solutions will meet the requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Launch a new Amazon Aurora MySQL database. Create an Aurora Auto Scaling policy and apply it to the Amazon Aurora DB cluster to automatically scale Aurora read replicas.
Launch a new Amazon Aurora MySQL database. Create an Aurora Auto Scaling policy that will automatically scale the Aurora writer instances

Use an Auto Scaling Group (ASG) for the EC2 instances. Attach the ASG to a Network Load Balancer (NLB). Enable sticky sessions and select Least Outstanding Requests (LOR) as the load balancing algorithm.

Use an Auto Scaling Group (ASG) for the EC2 instances. Attach the ASG to an Application Load Balancer (ALB). Enable sticky sessions and select round-robin as the load balancing algorithm for the target groups.
Use an Auto Scaling Group (ASG) for the EC2 instances. Attach the ASG to an Application Load Balancer (ALB). Enable Client Port preservation and select round-robin as the load balancing algorithm.

explanation.text:
Options <<1>> and <<4>> are the intended elastic application/read-tier design. An Auto Scaling group can add application instances, and Aurora Auto Scaling adds or removes reader instances; it does not horizontally scale a provisioned writer by adding writable instances. Route eligible reads through the appropriate reader endpoint and separately size or scale the writer. Load-balancer stickiness may keep a user on an instance but does not make in-memory session state durable during instance failure or scale-in; externalize important state. The answer is valid for a read-heavy growth pattern with independently adequate writer capacity, not unrestricted automatic scaling of every database operation.

https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/AuroraUserGuide/Aurora.Integrating.AutoScaling.html

question:
A forecasting agency is struggling to meet the Service Level Agreement (SLA) of its online platform. To avoid penalties and maintain credibility, they aim to develop a recovery plan that assures a Recovery Time Objective (RTO) of no more than 30 minutes.

Their platform runs on an Auto Scaling Group (ASG) connected to an Application Load Balancer (ALB). Data is stored in an Amazon RDS PostgreSQL database. An identical environment exists in a secondary region where the ASG’s capacity limits are set to zero. A read replica of the RDS database is deployed in this backup region as well. A Route 53 alias record is configured to route domain traffic to the ALB.

The agency cannot afford an active-active failover and is opting for a more cost-effective way of switching over to the backup region.

Which strategy would meet these requirements?

options.text: Configure Route 53 application health checks, CloudWatch alarm transitions, and SNS/Lambda recovery orchestration. On a confirmed primary failure, promote the secondary-Region database replica and scale the secondary Auto Scaling group. Make the secondary failover record eligible only after the promoted database and application are ready, then route traffic to the secondary ALB. Test DNS caching, promotion time, replication lag, and split-brain prevention.

Create a Lambda function that updates the ASG’s capacity limits and promotes the read replica to primary in the secondary Region. Set up a CloudWatch alarm that triggers the function when the HTTPCode_ELB_502_Count ALB metric becomes greater than or equal to 1.

Update the routing policy of the alias record to Weight with a value of 100. Create a new alias record for the application’s domain with a Weight routing policy initialized to 0. Adjust the Auto Scaling Group (ASG) in the secondary Region to match the capacity limits of the ASG in the primary Region. Create a Lambda function for weight adjustment and read replica promotion. Set up a Route 53 health check that sends an Amazon SNS notification to the Lambda function.

Set up an Amazon CloudWatch alarm that tracks the HTTPCode_Target_5XX_Count metric of the ALB in the primary Region. Create a secondary Route 53 record with identical values as the primary record. Adjust the Auto Scaling Group (ASG) in the secondary Region to match the capacity limits of the ASG in the primary Region. Create a Route 53 health check that sends an Amazon SNS notification to a Lambda function that will promote the read replica to the primary.

explanation.text:
The corrected option <<1>> uses a Route 53 health check with a CloudWatch alarm and SNS-triggered recovery orchestration. Route 53 health checks do not directly publish arbitrary SNS actions without that integration. Promote the replica and verify it is writable, bring up the application capacity, and only then expose the secondary as healthy for DNS routing. Fence the former primary to avoid split-brain writes, and make recovery idempotent. A long orchestration should use Step Functions/automation rather than assume one Lambda can wait indefinitely. DNS propagation, client caching, database promotion, capacity availability, and startup time must be included in an exercised 30-minute RTO; Route 53 alone does not provide that guarantee.

AWS references checked on 2026-09-13 (supporting the principal distinctions above):
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/USER_ReadRepl.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/step-functions/latest/dg/connect-to-resource.html

question:
A company runs an auction website using AWS Fargate fronted by an Application Load Balancer (ALB). The company manages an Amazon Route 53 hosted zone for its domain, which it presents to users. The domain is linked to a CloudFront distribution that points to the ALB as the origin.

Lately, there have been reports of intermittent HTTP 502 (Bad Gateway) errors. Initial investigation revealed that a misconfiguration in the Fargate task definition is causing the problem. This results in users seeing the ALB’s default error page.

To improve user experience, the company wants users to be redirected to a custom error page while they troubleshoot the issue. The solution must be achieved in the least amount of operational overhead.

Which solution would meet the requirements?

options.text: Store a static error page in a private S3 bucket and configure the bucket REST endpoint as a CloudFront origin protected by OAC. Add a cache behavior for the error-page path and configure a custom CloudFront error response to serve that page for the relevant origin 502 errors.

Create a Lambda function that adds a redirection rule to the path of the error page within the application. Configure a CloudWatch alarm to trigger this Lambda function when the Application Load Balancer (ALB) metric HTTPCode_Target_5XX_Count registers a value of one.

Upload the error HTML page to an Amazon S3 bucket and enable static website hosting. Update the existing Route 53 record by adding a failover policy that routes traffic to the S3 website endpoint when health checks become unhealthy.
Modify the Application Load Balancer’s rules by adding a condition for the path /*. Configure a fixed-response action that returns a 502 response code and a custom error message in the response body.

explanation.text:
Option <<1>> is correct after replacing the incompatible S3 website/OAC combination. Store the maintenance/error page in a private S3 bucket used through its REST origin, protect it with OAC, and configure a cache behavior for the error-page path. Configure CloudFront's custom error response to retrieve that page for the relevant origin error status. An S3 website endpoint cannot use OAC. A custom error response is not an origin-group failover policy and does not repair the application; choose response status and error-caching duration intentionally, without accidentally presenting a failed transaction as a successful one.

AWS references checked on 2026-09-13 (supporting the principal distinctions above):
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/private-content-restricting-access-to-s3.html

question:
A company uses AWS Organizations to manage hundreds of AWS accounts. The company plans to designate a central network account where a shared VPC will be created. Accounts under the Customers Organization Unit (OU) are allowed to create resources on the shared VPC, but they should not be able to manage it.

The AWS Security Hub has also been configured to provide the company with a comprehensive view of their security state in AWS and to help them verify their AWS workloads against security industry standards and best practices. There’s also a Security Hub administrator account that has already been designated in AWS Organizations to view data from its member accounts.

Which combination of steps would meet the company’s objectives? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Create a service control policy (SCP) within AWS Organizations and attach it to the Customers OU. This SCP should contain statements for denying management actions to a VPC.
Configure the management account to enable AWS Resource Access Manager (RAM) resource sharing with AWS Organizations.

Create a separate VPC within each individual account in the Customers OU. Set up a Resource Access Manager (RAM) resource share for a Transit Gateway in the management account and share it with the Customers OU. Establish VPC peering connections between all VPCs.
Use AWS Resource Access Manager (RAM) to create a resource share in the VPC-owning central networking account. Include all subnets of the shared VPC and set the Customers OU as the principal.

Configure a managed prefix list in the central network account, specifying the IP ranges that align with the desired network configuration. Use AWS Resource Access Manager (RAM) to share this prefix list with the Customers OU.

explanation.text:
Options <<2>> and <<4>> implement VPC sharing once the account ownership is corrected. Enable sharing with AWS Organizations from the management account. Create the actual RAM resource share in the account that owns the VPC/subnets, typically the central networking member account, and share eligible subnets with the intended organization/OU/accounts. The organization management account does not become the owner of another account's subnets. Participants deploy supported resources into the shared subnets; the VPC owner continues to manage shared network infrastructure. RAM does not itself prevent a participant from creating additional VPCs; use separate governance controls for that requirement.

question:
A company hosts an e-commerce application on an Auto Scaling group (ASG) of EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB). The ASG is set to maintain 10 EC2 instances at all times. It uses Elastic Load Balancing (ELB) health checks to detect and replace any unhealthy instances. Each EC2 instance has a CloudWatch agent installed that sends application logs to Amazon CloudWatch Logs at 5-minute intervals.

The operations team is unable to recover logs that were stored in terminated instances. This prevents them from conducting proper troubleshooting. For this reason, they require a solution that can automatically collect and back up relevant log data from instances that are about to be terminated.

Which solution would meet the requirements?

options.text: Create a shell script for backing up log data to an S3 bucket. Install the script to the EC2 instance’s user data. Run the script using a Lambda function via Remote Call Procedure (RPC). Create an Amazon EventBridge rule that invokes a Lambda function when an instance is in the Terminating state.

Change the interval at which the CloudWatch Logs agent sends data to 1 minute. Increase the deregistration delay of the Application Load Balancer. SSH into the instance to run the script for backing up the log data to an S3 bucket.

Add an autoscaling:EC2_INSTANCE_TERMINATING lifecycle hook to the Auto Scaling group and route its event through EventBridge to a Lambda orchestration function. Use Systems Manager SendCommand to execute a Command document that uploads remaining logs to S3. Monitor the command, send lifecycle heartbeats when needed, and complete the lifecycle action after success or a deliberately handled failure. Use continuous log shipping as the primary protection against crashes that bypass normal termination.

Use an AWS Systems Manager Automation document to create the script for backing up log data to an Amazon S3 bucket. Create an OpsItem for EC2 termination events in AWS Systems Manager OpsCenter. Configure a remediation runbook that calls the CompleteLifecycleAction Auto Scaling API with ABANDON to pause the termination of instance and SendCommand System Manager API to run the automation document.

explanation.text:
Option <<3>> is the intended termination-hook workflow after correcting the Systems Manager document type. A lifecycle hook pauses scale-in; EventBridge invokes automation that uses SendCommand with a Command document such as AWS-RunShellScript to upload the required logs, then calls CompleteLifecycleAction with CONTINUE. StartAutomationExecution is used for an Automation runbook, not SendCommand. Send lifecycle heartbeats if necessary and account for hook timeout/failure. This process is best effort when an instance or its agent is unhealthy; continually streaming critical logs is more robust than relying only on a final upload. ABANDON does not mean that a terminating instance is permanently preserved.

AWS references checked on 2026-09-13 (supporting the principal distinctions above):
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/systems-manager/latest/userguide/run-command.html

question:
A company that operates a multi-cloud environment uses an on-premises Microsoft Active Directory for user authentication. As part of its expansion plans, the company is preparing to launch services in AWS. They want to leverage its existing Active Directory to control the permissions of those who wish to access AWS resources. There’s already a Direct Connect connection in place between the company’s on-premises data center and its AWS networks.

The company wants to enforce a security policy where access to accounts is regulated based on user group membership and assigned roles. Moreover, they must have the ability to manage user identities in a centralized location.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Create an AWS Cognito User Pool and connect it to Active Directory using SAML 2.0. Use the System for Cross-domain Identity Management (SCIM) v2.0 protocol to enable automatic provisioning. Use a Cognito Identity pool to grant access to the AWS accounts.

Create a PowerShell script that creates a separate identity provider for connecting to the Active Directory. Set up IAM user accounts manually in each AWS account and synchronize them with the identities in Active Directory.

Federate IAM Identity Center with a SAML 2.0 identity provider backed by the existing Active Directory. Configure a supported provisioning method, using SCIM where the identity provider supports it. Assign users/groups and permission sets to the appropriate AWS accounts; configure trusted attributes for access control and IAM ABAC policies within those assigned permissions.

Export the user list from the on-premises Active Directory and import it into a new AWS Directory Service for Microsoft Active Directory (AWS Managed Microsoft AD). Configure trust relationships between AWS Managed Microsoft AD and AWS accounts. Use AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) to manage user access and permissions.

explanation.text:
Option <<3>> is the intended central federation design after distinguishing Active Directory from a SAML identity provider. Integrate IAM Identity Center with an actual SAML 2.0 IdP, such as AD FS backed by Active Directory, and configure provisioning using supported SCIM integration or another supported process. AD itself is not a SAML issuer, and an arbitrary AD FS deployment does not automatically provide SCIM. Alternatively use a supported Identity Center Active Directory identity-source integration. Assign groups/users to accounts and permission sets; attribute-based access control can then refine supported resource permissions. ABAC attributes do not replace the account assignments or authorize every AWS service uniformly.

https://docs.aws.amazon.com/singlesignon/latest/userguide/manage-your-identity-source-idp.html

question:
An enterprise uses AWS Organizations to manage hundreds of AWS accounts. Each division falls under a corresponding Organizational Unit (OU) with different permissions for accessing AWS services.

The analytics division has a data analysis tool within each VPC where the enterprise has its workloads running. This tool operates on EC2 instances and runs at least once a week. The collected data is sent to an AWS account dedicated to the analytics division and stored in an Amazon Redshift data warehouse.

The accounting division needs to determine how much it costs to run the analysis tool, so they can bill the analytics division accordingly. All analytics-related resources are already tagged using the AWS tag "expenseUnit": "analytics".

Which set of actions would meet the requirements?

options.text: Enable the user-defined "expenseUnit": "analytics" cost allocation tag on the Billing and Cost Management console of the management account. Use AWS Cost and Usage Reports to generate the monthly billing report to an S3 bucket. Filter the data using tag breakdown to get the total cost associated with the resources tagged with "expenseUnit": "analytics".

In the AWS account of the analytics division, enable the user-defined "expenseUnit": "analytics" cost allocation tag on the Billing and Cost Management console. Generate the monthly billing report using AWS Cost and Usage Reports and save it to an S3 bucket. Use Amazon Athena to calculate the total cost associated with the resources tagged with "expenseUnit": "analytics".

In the AWS account of the accounting division, enable the user-defined "expenseUnit": "analytics" cost allocation tag on the Billing and Cost Management console. In the management account, generate the monthly billing report using AWS Cost and Usage Reports and save it to an S3 bucket. Filter the data using tag breakdown to get the total cost associated with the resources tagged with "expenseUnit": "analytics".

Create an AWS Resource group of resources tagged with the "expenseUnit": "analytics" in the management account. Generate the monthly billing report using AWS Cost and Usage Reports and save it to an S3 bucket. Use Amazon Athena to calculate the total cost associated with the resources tagged with "expenseUnit": "analytics".

explanation.text:
A tag is a label that you or AWS assigns to an AWS resource. Each tag consists of a key and a value. For each resource, each tag key must be unique, and each tag key can have only one value. You can use tags to organize your resources and cost allocation tags to track your AWS costs on a detailed level.

After you or AWS applies tags to your AWS resources (such as Amazon EC2 instances or Amazon S3 buckets) and you activate the tags in the Billing and Cost Management console, AWS generates a cost allocation report as a comma-separated value (CSV file) with your usage and costs grouped by your active tags. You can apply tags that represent business categories (such as cost centers, application names, or owners) to organize your costs across multiple services.

In the scenario, the organization is using AWS Organizations to manage multiple accounts, necessitating cross-account cost calculation. The management account, with its organization-wide visibility, is best suited for this task. By enabling the "expenseUnit": "analytics" cost allocation tag at this level, all analytics-related resources across accounts can be tracked. AWS Cost and Usage Reports can then be generated from the management account, with data filtered by the tag, yielding the precise cost for running the analysis tool.

Hence, the correct answer is: Enable the user-defined "expenseUnit": "analytics" cost allocation tag on the Billing and Cost Management console of the management account. Use AWS Cost and Usage Reports to generate the monthly billing report to an S3 bucket. Filter the data using tag breakdown to get the total cost associated with the resources tagged with "expenseUnit": "analytics".

Only a management account in an organization and single accounts that aren’t members of an organization have access to the cost allocation tags manager in the Billing and Cost Management console. Hence, the following options are both incorrect:

– In the AWS account of the analytics division, enable the user-defined "expenseUnit": "analytics" cost allocation tag on the Billing and Cost Management console. Generate the monthly billing report using AWS Cost and Usage Reports and save it to an S3 bucket. Use Amazon Athena to calculate the total cost associated with the resources tagged with "expenseUnit": "analytics".

– In the AWS account of the accounting division, enable the user-defined "expenseUnit": "analytics" cost allocation tag on the Billing and Cost Management console. In the management account, generate the monthly billing report using AWS Cost and Usage Reports and save it to an S3 bucket. Filter the data using tag breakdown to get the total cost associated with the resources tagged with "expenseUnit": "analytics".

The option that says: Create an AWS Resource group of resources tagged with the "expenseUnit": "analytics" in the management account. Generate the monthly billing report using AWS Cost and Usage Reports and save it to an S3 bucket. Use Amazon Athena to calculate the total cost associated with the resources tagged with "expenseUnit": "analytics" is incorrect. AWS Resource Groups are typically used to manage and automate tasks on a large collection of AWS resources at once. They are not primarily used for cost calculation purposes. It is more straightforward and accurate to use the AWS Cost and Usage Reports, which provide detailed cost information and allow filtering by tags.

https://docs.aws.amazon.com/awsaccountbilling/latest/aboutv2/cost-alloc-tags.html

https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/aws-cloud-financial-management/cost-allocation-blog-series-2-aws-generated-vs-user-defined-cost-allocation-tag/

Check out this AWS Billing and Cost Management Cheat sheet:

https://tutorialsdojo.com/aws-billing-and-cost-management/

question:
A global corporation manages numerous operation groups, each with unique IT requirements. The corporation uses AWS Organizations to assign individual groups to their respective Organizational Units (OUs). Each OU contains thousands of AWS accounts. A solutions architect is tasked with designing a solution that allows each OU to view and analyze a detailed breakdown of AWS usage and costs for its member accounts.

Which set of actions will satisfy the requirements?

options.text: Use AWS Systems Manager OpsCenter in the management account to generate an AWS Cost and Usage Report (CUR). Store the CUR in an Amazon S3 bucket and visualize it on an Amazon QuickSight dashboard.
Create an AWS Cost and Usage Report (CUR) in the management account. Store the CUR in a central Amazon S3 bucket and visualize it on an Amazon QuickSight dashboard.
Use AWS Trusted Advisor in the management account to generate an AWS Cost and Usage Report (CUR). Store the CUR in an Amazon S3 bucket and visualize it on a custom CloudWatch Dashboard.

Create a Lambda function in the management account. Configure the function to create an AWS Cost and Usage Report (CUR) in the member's account. Schedule the function using Amazon EventBridge.Store the CUR in a central Amazon S3 bucket and visualize it on a custom CloudWatch Dashboard.

explanation.text:
Option <<2>> is the intended centralized chargeback reporting design. Use the management-account Cost and Usage Report/Data Exports with account identifiers, query the data, and join account IDs to an explicit organizational-unit/business-unit mapping. An OU is not automatically a universal resource-level cost allocation field, and historical account-to-OU membership may need to be retained if accounts move. Configure QuickSight row-level security or separately scoped datasets/reports so each department sees only authorized costs. Merely building one organization-wide dashboard does not enforce departmental isolation. Use activated cost allocation tags for within-account attribution where supported.

question:
A company manages thousands of AWS accounts using AWS Organizations. To ensure compliance and maintain a uniform environment, each member account requires a standardized Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) with specific networking configurations.

The company’s DevOps team has already prepared an AWS CloudFormation template for creating the VPC. They want the deployment of the CloudFormation template to be automated in a consistent manner across the organization. Moreover, the template must be automatically deployed in newly joined accounts.

Which combination of actions will meet the requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Enable CloudFormation StackSet as a trusted service on AWS Organizations.
Enable Service Catalog as a trusted service on AWS Organizations. Provision service-managed permissions.

In the management account, set up a stack set using the CloudFormation template. Use the service-managed permission model to create the stack. Activate Automatic deployment and set the Organizations as the deployment target.

In the member accounts, set up a stack set using the CloudFormation template. Use a self-managed permission model to create the stack. Use Stackset drift detection to enable deployment to new accounts. Specify each Organization Unit (OU) as a deployment target.
Create a portfolio in AWS Service Catalog and associate the CloudFormation template as a product. Grant access to this portfolio to all AWS accounts in the organization.

explanation.text:
AWS CloudFormation StackSets extends the functionality of stacks by enabling you to create, update, or delete stacks across multiple accounts and regions with a single operation. Using an administrator account, you define and manage an AWS CloudFormation template and use the template as the basis for provisioning stacks into selected target accounts across specified regions.

A stack set lets you create stacks in AWS accounts across regions by using a single AWS CloudFormation template. All the resources included in each stack are defined by the stack set’s AWS CloudFormation template. As you create the stack set, you specify the template to use, as well as any parameters and capabilities that the template requires.

In the scenario, in order for StackSets to have the necessary permissions to perform operations in AWS Organizations’ accounts, it must be enabled as a trusted service. To ensure the template is automatically deployed to all accounts (including newly joined ones), a stack set should be created in the management account with service-managed permissions. The AWS Organizations should be set as the deployment target, and automatic deployments should be enabled.

Hence, the correct answers are:

– Enable CloudFormation StackSet as a trusted service on AWS Organizations.

– In the management account, set up a stack set using the CloudFormation template. Use the service-managed permission model to create the stack. Activate Automatic deployment and set the Organizations as the deployment target.

The option that says: Enable Service Catalog as a trusted service on AWS Organizations. Provision service-managed permissions is incorrect. While AWS Service Catalog can be used to create and manage catalogs of IT services, it doesn’t inherently offer a solution for automatic deployments across AWS accounts in an organization, especially for newly joined accounts. The requirement in the question is specifically about deploying AWS CloudFormation templates across multiple accounts and not about managing a service catalog.

The option that says: In the member accounts, set up a stack set using the CloudFormation template. Use a self-managed permission model to create the stack. Use Stackset drift detection to enable deployment to new accounts. Specify each Organization Unit (OU) as a deployment target is incorrect. Setting up a stack set in each member account manually defeats the purpose of AWS CloudFormation StackSets, which is designed to manage resources centrally from a single AWS account. Additionally, StackSet drift detection is used for checking configuration consistency, not for enabling deployment to new accounts.

The option that says: Create a portfolio in AWS Service Catalog and associate the CloudFormation template as a product. Grant access to this portfolio to all AWS accounts in the organization is incorrect. While this option might provide a way to standardize the deployment of services, it still doesn’t address the need for automatic deployment, especially for new accounts joining the organization.

References:

https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSCloudFormation/latest/UserGuide/what-is-cfnstacksets.html

https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSCloudFormation/latest/UserGuide/stacksets-getting-started.html

Check out this AWS CloudFormation Cheat Sheet:

https://tutorialsdojo.com/aws-cloudformation/

question:
A company has a suite of services hosted on its on-premises data center. These services run on a network of virtualized Ubuntu and Windows servers. To benefit from AWS’ scaling capabilities, the company decides to migrate its entire system to AWS.

The migration strategy aims to precisely understand the actual usage and deeply analyze application components and the dependencies within its on-premises workload. The company also wants to right-size its Amazon EC2 instances to avoid unnecessary expenses for underutilized resources.

Which set of actions will meet the requirements?

options.text: Deploy the AWS Transform discovery tool in the on-premises environment to gather performance and usage information from physical servers and virtual machines. Use AWS Transform migration planning to group servers into applications and migration waves, and use AWS Transform migration assessments to generate EC2 right-sizing and cost recommendations.

Install the AWS Systems Manager Agent on both the physical servers and Virtual machines to perform an application-level assessment. Utilize Systems Manager Application Manager to logically separate servers into different applications. Input server size data into the AWS Pricing calculator and adhere to its recommendations.

Use AWS Transform MGN to install replication agents on the source servers and immediately start continuous block-level replication to AWS. After the servers are launched on EC2, use AWS Compute Optimizer to recommend instance sizes.

Deploy the AWS Transform discovery tool in the on-premises environment to gather performance and usage information from physical servers and virtual machines. Use AWS Transform migration planning to group servers into applications and migration waves. After the workloads are migrated to EC2, use AWS Compute Optimizer to generate EC2 right-sizing recommendations.

explanation.text:
AWS Transform is a service designed to accelerate and simplify the transformation of infrastructure, applications, and code through an intelligent AI experience. It offers specialized tools that streamline modernization and migration efforts across various workloads.

With AWS Transform, you can:

– Modernize and migrate IBM z/OS and Fujitsu GS21 to AWS

– Migrate VMware workloads to Amazon EC2

– Modernize .NET applications to Linux-ready cross-platform .NET

– Assess workloads for migration readiness

AWS Transform assists in offloading labor-intensive and complex transformation tasks during the discovery, planning, and execution phases to AI agents with expertise in various languages, frameworks, and infrastructures. This approach allows your teams to focus on innovation while efficiently transforming complex, large-scale projects through a unified web experience.

The AWS Transform discovery tool automatically identifies server inventory within your organization to prepare for migration. The tool supports VMware vCenter, Microsoft Hyper-V, and imported servers. To use the discovery tool, you’ll configure one or more discovery sources, let the tool run, and then review the results in the Discovered Inventory pane.

Once you’ve set up a discovery source, the discovery tool begins collecting information. The time required for the tool to analyze your network completely depends on the size of your environment. For a directional migration business case, you can utilize the Migration Portfolio Assessment (MPA) files that the tool generates once server collection is complete.

The Migration Planning job step within AWS Transform for VMware provides a collaborative, chat-based experience designed for planning large migrations. AWS Transform agents utilize AWS Prescriptive Guidance to assist customers in transitioning from analyzing on-premises data to finalizing migration wave plans.

Once the Discover on-premises data job successfully completes, AWS Transform employs the discovery data to categorize applications into migration waves. The service guides you through the steps of analyzing and scoping your servers, grouping them into applications, creating move groups, and developing migration waves. During the analysis of your on-premises environment, you can ask questions to gain insights into how AWS Transform evaluated your installed software, including aspects such as server dependencies and network architecture.

AWS Transform assessments help you evaluate the cost, feasibility, and business value of migrating your on-premises infrastructure to AWS. These assessments provide automated right-sizing recommendations, multi-scenario comparisons, and interactive refinements through chat.

You can use migration assessments to:

– Obtain cost estimates for Amazon RDS for SQL Server, Amazon EC2, Amazon EBS, Amazon S3, and Amazon FSx

– Receive automated right-sizing recommendations

– Assess business value and sustainability impact

– Compare multiple migration scenarios side by side

– Refine assessments interactively through chat

– Generate executive presentations and detailed reports

Hence, the correct answer is: Deploy the AWS Transform discovery tool in the on-premises environment to gather performance and usage information from physical servers and virtual machines. Use AWS Transform migration planning to group servers into applications and migration waves, and use AWS Transform migration assessments to generate EC2 right-sizing and cost recommendations.

The option that says: Install the AWS Systems Manager Agent on both the physical servers and Virtual machines to perform an application-level assessment. Utilize Systems Manager Application Manager to logically separate servers into different applications. Input server size data into the AWS Pricing calculator and adhere to its recommendations is incorrect. The AWS Systems Manager agent does not provide a deep understanding of current resource usage and application dependencies as the AWS Application Discovery Agent. AWS Systems Manager Application Manager is primarily designed for application lifecycle management, not necessarily for grouping servers into applications as part of a migration strategy. Also, the AWS Pricing calculator gives cost estimates based on input parameters but does not provide sophisticated EC2 instance sizing recommendations that are based on actual performance and usage data.

The option that says: Use AWS Transform MGN to install replication agents on the source servers and immediately start continuous block-level replication to AWS. After the servers are launched on EC2, use AWS Compute Optimizer to recommend instance sizes is incorrect because AWS Transform MGN is typically a rehost migration service that replicates source servers to AWS using block-level replication. This option begins replication immediately and skips the required discovery, dependency analysis, application grouping, and migration wave planning. In addition, AWS Compute Optimizer analyzes CloudWatch metrics from running AWS resources, so it is better suited for optimization after workloads are already running in AWS, not for the required pre-migration assessment.

The option that says: Deploy the AWS Transform discovery tool in the on-premises environment to gather performance and usage information from physical servers and virtual machines. Use AWS Transform migration planning to group servers into applications and migration waves. After the workloads are migrated to EC2, use AWS Compute Optimizer to generate EC2 right-sizing recommendations is incorrect because it correctly uses AWS Transform discovery and migration planning, but it delays right-sizing until after the workloads have already been migrated to Amazon EC2. AWS Compute Optimizer provides recommendations for optimal AWS resource utilization based on historical usage data. In this case, the company has not yet migrated to AWS, so there’s no historical usage data for the Compute Optimizer to base its recommendations on.

question:
A company has hundreds of AWS accounts in an organization in AWS Organizations. The accounts are associated with one of the three Organization Units (OU): PROD, DEV, and UAT. The company uses the vpc-sg-open-only-to-authorized-ports AWS Config managed rule, deployed as part of a Config conformance pack, to determine if a security group that allows incoming traffic at ‘0.0.0.0/0’ is created on any of the OUs. An Amazon SNS topic is configured to send email alerts to the security team when a security group is flagged as non-compliant.

There are critical security groups that must not be modified by users. The security team wants to prevent accounts in the PROD OU from altering the rules of these security groups.

Which solution would meet the requirements?

options.text: Apply a remediation action to the Config rule using the AWSConfigRemediation-RemoveUnrestrictedSourceIngressRules AWS System Manager Automation document.

Apply a tested SCP to the relevant member-account OU that denies unauthorized mutations of designated critical security groups, covering rule authorization, revocation, modification and deletion. Protect the identifying tags and use supported action/resource conditions for every covered API. Keep the Config control as a detective supplement.
Create a Service control policy (SCP) that denies the ec2:AuthorizeSecurityGroup* action with the “aws:SourceIp”: “0.0.0.0/0” condition key. Attach the SCP to the PROD OU.
Create an AWS Lambda function that calls the RevokeSecurityGroupIngress on security groups that have an inbound rule allowing traffic from 0.0.0.0/0. Subscribe the Lambda function to the SNS topic.

explanation.text:
Option <<2>> is the intended preventive mechanism, but a guardrail protecting critical security groups must cover all relevant mutation paths, not only AuthorizeSecurityGroupIngress/Egress. Include revocation, rule modification, deletion, and protection of the classification tags, using action/resource/condition combinations that those APIs actually support. Test the policy against security-group-rule resources as well as security-group resources. A tag-based deny that permits users to remove the protected tag is bypassable. aws:SourceIp refers to the API caller's source, not the CIDR entered into a security-group rule. The Config rule vpc-sg-open-only-to-authorized-ports permits public access on designated authorized ports; it is not a rule declaring every 0.0.0.0/0 rule noncompliant.

question:
A company has a marketing service that schedules and posts content on a social media platform. The service currently runs on a collection of Amazon EC2 instances within an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB). This ALB responds to webhook calls from the social media platform when specific events occur, such as mentions, shares, or specific hashtag uses. The company wants to migrate this service to a serverless architecture to lessen administrative overhead.

Which action would be the most operationally efficient way to meet the requirements?

options.text: Run the service using AWS Lambda. Generate a Lambda Function URL for each webhook. Configure the platform to send webhook calls to the function URLs.
Use AWS Lambda to run the service. Create a single AWS AppSync GraphQL API endpoint and connect it to the Lambda functions. Configure the platform to send webhook calls to the AppSync endpoint.

Replace the Amazon EC2 instances with AWS Fargate tasks. Create an Amazon Gateway HTTP API and integrate it with the Application Load Balancer. Configure the platform to send webhook calls to the HTTP API endpoint.

Run the service using AWS Lambda. Create an Amazon Gateway REST API that uses proxy integration with AWS Lambda. Create an API resource for each webhook. Configure the platform to send webhook calls to the REST API endpoint.

explanation.text:
Lambda function URLs are HTTP(S) endpoints dedicated to your Lambda function. You can easily create and set up a function URL using the Lambda console or API. Once created, Lambda generates a unique URL endpoint for your use.

Function URLs are dual stack-enabled, supporting IPv4 and IPv6. After you configure a function URL for your function, you can invoke your function through its HTTP(S) endpoint via a web browser, curl, Postman, or any HTTP client.

In the scenario, exposing Lambda functions directly using function URLS eliminates the need for intermediaries like Amazon API Gateway. This approach significantly simplifies the architecture, reduces latency, and lessens administrative overhead. Each webhook can be configured to send calls to specific Lambda function URLs, providing a response mechanism for various social media events.

Hence, the correct answer is: Run the service using AWS Lambda. Generate a Lambda Function URL for each webhook. Configure the platform to send webhook calls to the function URLs.

The option that says: Use AWS Lambda to run the service. Create a single AWS AppSync GraphQL API endpoint and connect it to the Lambda functions. Configure the platform to send webhook calls to the AppSync endpoint is incorrect. AWS AppSync is a just managed service that uses GraphQL to make it easy for applications to get exactly the data they need. While you can use it with Lambda, this solution is not as straightforward as directly triggering Lambda functions using function URLs. Using AppSync might introduce unnecessary complexity for this use case which is about responding to webhook calls from a social media platform, not handling GraphQL queries from a client application.

The option that says: Replace the Amazon EC2 instances with AWS Fargate tasks. Create an Amazon Gateway HTTP API and integrate it with the Application Load Balancer. Configure the platform to send webhook calls to the HTTP API endpoint is incorrect. While AWS Fargate is a serverless compute engine for containers, it wouldn’t be the most efficient choice in the scenario. Using Fargate would require you to containerize the application, which adds an additional layer of development and management overhead

The option that says: Run the service using AWS Lambda. Create an Amazon Gateway REST API that uses proxy integration with AWS Lambda. Create an API resource for each webhook. Configure the platform to send webhook calls to the REST API endpoint is incorrect. Although this option could work, it introduces additional complexity by using Amazon API Gateway as an intermediary. In this scenario, a fully-fledged REST API is not necessary. Instead of creating an API resource for each webhook, it would be simpler and more efficient to directly trigger specific AWS Lambda functions thru Lambda function URLs.

question:
A solutions architect is planning the migration of hundreds of Hyper-V servers from an on-premises data center to AWS. To design an effective AWS infrastructure, the solutions architect needs to understand the type of running processes, CPU and memory load, and network dependencies between each server.

What steps should the architect take to collect and analyze this data? (Select THREE.)

options.text: Create a custom PowerShell script to collect basic server inventory from the Hyper-V servers. Upload the generated inventory file to AWS Transform for migration assessment.
Deploy the AWS Transform discovery tool on the on-premises Hyper-V servers to collect server data.
Install the Amazon CloudWatch agent on the on-premises Hyper-V servers to collect system-level metrics. Use AWS System Manager OpsCenter to export the collected data to an Amazon S3 bucket.
Create a migration assessment job in AWS Transform by using the discovery data.
Create an AWS Glue Extract, Transform, Load (ETL) job to prepare the data for querying. Use Amazon Athena to run SQL queries on the transformed data for deeper analysis.
Use AWS Transform migration assessment results, chat-based analysis, and generated reports to evaluate right-sizing recommendations, dependencies, costs, and migration wave plans.

explanation.text:
AWS Transform is a service designed to accelerate and simplify the transformation of infrastructure, applications, and code through an intelligent AI experience. It offers specialized tools that streamline modernization and migration efforts across various workloads.

With AWS Transform, you can:

- Modernize and migrate IBM z/OS and Fujitsu GS21 to AWS
- Migrate VMware workloads to Amazon EC2
- Modernize .NET applications to Linux-ready cross-platform .NET
- Assess workloads for migration readiness

AWS Transform assists in offloading labor-intensive and complex transformation tasks during the discovery, planning, and execution phases to AI agents with expertise in various languages, frameworks, and infrastructures. This approach allows your teams to focus on innovation while efficiently transforming complex, large-scale projects through a unified web experience.

The AWS Transform discovery tool automatically identifies server inventory within your organization to prepare for migration. The tool supports VMware vCenter, Microsoft Hyper-V, and imported servers. To use the discovery tool, you’ll configure one or more discovery sources, let the tool run, and then review the results in the Discovered Inventory pane.

Once you’ve set up a discovery source, the discovery tool begins collecting information. The time required for the tool to analyze your network completely depends on the size of your environment. For a directional migration business case, you can utilize the Migration Portfolio Assessment (MPA) files that the tool generates once server collection is complete.

AWS Transform assessments help you evaluate the cost, feasibility, and business value of migrating your on-premises infrastructure to AWS. These assessments provide automated right-sizing recommendations, multi-scenario comparisons, and interactive refinements through chat.

You can use migration assessments to:

– Obtain cost estimates for Amazon RDS for SQL Server, Amazon EC2, Amazon EBS, Amazon S3, and Amazon FSx

– Receive automated right-sizing recommendations

– Assess business value and sustainability impact

– Compare multiple migration scenarios side by side

– Refine assessments interactively through chat

– Generate executive presentations and detailed reports

Hence, the correct answers are:

– Deploy the AWS Transform discovery tool on the on-premises Hyper-V servers to collect server data.

– Create a migration assessment job in AWS Transform by using the discovery data.

– Use AWS Transform migration assessment results, chat-based analysis, and generated reports to evaluate right-sizing recommendations, dependencies, costs, and migration wave plans.

The option that says: Create a custom PowerShell script to collect basic server inventory from the Hyper-V servers. Upload the generated inventory file to AWS Transform for migration assessment is incorrect. While it’s technically possible, this approach is significantly more complex and less comprehensive than using the AWS Transform discovery tool.

The option that says: Install the Amazon CloudWatch agent on the on-premises Hyper-V servers to collect system-level metrics. Use AWS System Manager OpsCenter to export the collected data to an Amazon S3 bucket is incorrect. Although CloudWatch can be used to collect system-level metrics, it doesn’t provide detailed, in-depth discovery information needed for migration planning, such as dependencies, configurations, and utilization of on-premises servers. Furthermore, AWS Systems Manager OpsCenter typically provides a central location where you can manage and resolve operational issues, but it’s not a migration tool.

The option that says: Create an AWS Glue Extract, Transform, Load (ETL) job to prepare the data for querying. Use Amazon Athena to run SQL queries on the transformed data for deeper analysis is incorrect. AWS Glue’s ETL capabilities are unnecessary for this task because AWS Transform primarily provides the data in a format that is ready for analysis. There is no need to transform the data before running SQL queries.
